notes.title: Start here: sprint assignment and completion under concurrency
notes.body:
This quest studies one service file: `apps/api/src/services/sprint.service.js` in a Jira-like app. Two writes matter most. `assignIssueToSprint` moves an issue into a sprint (or back to the backlog), and `completeSprint` closes an ACTIVE sprint and moves its unfinished issues somewhere else. Both can run at the same time for the same data, so the code layers several protections.

Read in this order. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md` follows one request from the backlog page to the database. `02-CONCEPTS.md` separates isolation, state guards and stale-edit tokens. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` walks completion line by line. `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md` and `07-TRACE-LAB.md` show the race tests. `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` checks the answers against source.

Each chapter ends with Goal/Check exercises. Several quiz questions ask which Check belongs to which Goal, so read those lists carefully.

notes.title: Concept: isolation, state guards and a version token are different tools
notes.body:
It is tempting to say "the transaction makes it safe". This course insists on separating several ideas, each with its own test.

Isolation: `serializable()` in the service runs the work at the Serializable isolation level, where PostgreSQL may refuse an unsafe interleaving of two transactions. Read the helper and write down exactly which errors it treats as retryable, how many times the work can run, and what reaches the caller when the attempts run out or a different error is thrown.

State guards: a transition such as completion needs the row to still be in a certain state. Find where each write states that requirement, and work out what the losing request of a race sees.

Version tokens: `expectedUpdatedAt` asks whether the row is still the version the browser saw. Find every function that uses it, note whether the comparison happens in an earlier read or inside the write itself, and compare the two writers.

Ownership checks (is this sprint in this project?) are a further, independent rule.

excerpts.quote: # Separate isolation, state guards, and stale edits
Each mechanism protects a distinct invariant and should retain its own test.

readMore.why: The full assignIssueToSprint excerpt with all mechanisms in one function.

notes.title: Concept: one-row rules versus rules that span rows
notes.body:
Some rules can be checked by looking at one row: a sprint must be in the right state before a transition, and it may need at least one issue. Those live in a small state machine, `apps/api/src/domain/sprint-state-machine.js`, as a table of transitions.

Other rules span rows, for example "how many sprints of a project may be ACTIVE at once". Think about why an application check that reads other rows first is fragile when two requests run at the same moment.

Then go and find how this repo enforces that cross-row rule. Look in the sprint migration under `apps/api/prisma/migrations/` for any index or constraint that mentions sprint state, and read `startSprint` in the service: which error, if any, does it catch, which Prisma error code does it test for, and what does it turn that into? Write your timeline for two simultaneous starts before you read the tests.

notes.title: An unknown action is a conflict, not a crash
notes.body:
**Key: it throws a 409 conflict with Unknown sprint action "cancel".**

`assertTransition` looks the action up in `TRANSITIONS`. When there is no row, `if (!t) throw conflict(...)` runs. `conflict()` builds an `ApiError` with code `CONFLICT`, and `ERROR_CODES` maps that to 409.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Returns the current state*: nothing returns early; a missing row throws.
- *Plain Error, 500*: the function uses the domain `conflict` helper, not `new Error`. (A plain Error is what `can()` in the policy throws for an unknown policy action, a different function.)
- *Returns null*: the function either throws or returns `t.to`.

readMore.why: How the CONFLICT code becomes HTTP 409.

notes.title: The report reads the sprint's issues as they are now
notes.body:
**Key: committed 5, completed 5, total 1, with unfinished empty.**

Completion's bulk move wrote `sprintId: null` (the 'backlog' destination) on the 3-point issue, because it was not in a DONE column. `sprintReport` keeps no snapshot: it reads `prisma.issue.findMany` with `where: { sprintId: sprint.id }`. Only the DONE 5-point issue still points at S, so it is the whole report.

Why the others are wrong:
- *committed 8, total 2*: the 3-point issue no longer belongs to S.
- *completed 8*: completion moves unfinished work out; it does not mark it done.
- *all zeros*: issues in DONE columns are not moved, so the 5-point one stays.

notes.title: A missing estimate counts as zero, not as an error
notes.body:
**Key: committed 8, completed 5, total 3, and two unfinished issues.**

Both sums use `sum + (i.storyPoints ?? 0)`, so the unestimated issue adds 0. `total` is `issues.length`, which counts all three. `unfinished` keeps every issue whose column is not a DONE column: the 3-point issue and the unestimated one.

Why the others are wrong:
- *total 2*: nothing filters out issues with null points.
- *one unfinished issue*: the null issue is also in progress, so it is unfinished too.
- *409*: the report never throws on a missing estimate.

readMore.why: The three report figures and the unfinished list.

notes.title: 'backlog' is a word, not a sprint id
notes.body:
**Key: their sprintId becomes null, because 'backlog' is mapped to null first.**

Before the transaction starts, line 79 turns `'backlog'` into `null` (and a missing value into `null` too). With `destination` null, the whole `if (destination)` block is skipped, and the bulk move writes `data: { sprintId: destination }`, which is `null`: the backlog.

Why the others are wrong:
- *404 Destination sprint*: the lookup is inside `if (destination)` and never runs.
- *literal 'backlog'*: the string was replaced by `null` on line 79.
- *409 planned sprint*: that check is also inside the skipped block.

readMore.why: The schema comment: a sprint id, 'backlog', or null.

notes.title: Leaving a completed sprint is allowed
notes.body:
**Key: it moves the issue to the backlog, since the sprint checks need a sprintId.**

The sprint lookup and the `COMPLETED` rejection live inside `if (sprintId)`. They guard the sprint the issue is going *to*. With `sprintId` null they are skipped, the token matches, and `updateMany` writes `sprintId: null` with a new `updatedAt`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *409, cannot leave*: no code looks at the sprint the issue is coming from.
- *404 for null*: the lookup is skipped, so nothing can be not found.
- *updatedAt left alone*: every successful assignment writes `nextUpdatedAt`.

excerpts.quote: // sprintId null = move to backlog. Validate the sprint belongs to the project. if (sprintId) {

notes.title: A member with the wrong role gets 403
notes.body:
**Key: 403, Your role (VIEWER) is not permitted to sprint:manage.**

`assignIssueToSprint` calls `loadProject(projectKey, actorId, 'sprint:manage')`, which calls `authorize`. `requireMembership` finds the viewer in the member map, so there is no 404. Then `can('VIEWER', 'sprint:manage')` is false, because the policy lists only `ADMIN` and `MEMBER`, and `authorize` throws `forbidden(...)`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *404*: that is for non-members, whose role lookup comes back empty.
- *200*: reading sprints (`sprint:read`) and managing them are separate actions.
- *409*: the token is never checked; authorization fails first.

excerpts.quote: if (!can(role, action)) { throw forbidden(`Your role (${role}) is not permitted to ${action}`);

readMore.why: Who may read and who may manage sprints.

notes.title: The per-sprint guard runs before the write
notes.body:
**Key: 409 "Cannot start a sprint with no issues", from the state machine.**

`startSprint` loads the sprint with its issue count and calls `assertTransition('start', sprint.state, { issueCount })` on line 54. The start transition's guard returns the no-issues message when the count is 0, and `assertTransition` throws it as a conflict. The update on line 64, where the one-active-sprint index could fire, is never reached.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Another sprint is already active*: that needs the update to run, and it does not.
- *404 Sprint*: the lookup filters by id and project only.
- *It starts*: the guard belongs to the start transition; completion has no guards.

excerpts.quote: (ctx) => ((ctx.issueCount ?? 0) > 0 ? null : 'Cannot start a sprint with no issues'),

readMore.why: The order: lookup, guard, then the update.

notes.title: A sprint cannot be its own destination
notes.body:
**Key: 409 "Unfinished issues cannot stay in the completed sprint".**

Inside `if (destination)`, the first test is `destination === sprint.id`. It throws before the destination lookup, before the PLANNED check, and before any write.

Why the others are wrong:
- *can only move to a planned sprint*: S is ACTIVE, so that check would fail too, but the self-check comes first.
- *200, issues stay*: completion never leaves unfinished issues in the completed sprint.
- *404 Destination sprint*: the lookup is never reached; it would find S anyway.

excerpts.quote: if (destination === sprint.id) { throw conflict('Unfinished issues cannot stay in the completed sprint');

notes.title: Re-assigning to the same sprint is still a write
notes.body:
**Key: the issue comes back, with its updatedAt moved forward.**

No line compares the issue's current `sprintId` with the requested one. The sprint exists and is not COMPLETED, so the checks pass. `updateMany` matches the token and writes the same `sprintId` with `nextUpdatedAt`, and the function returns the re-read issue (the controller sends 200).

Why the others are wrong:
- *unchanged*: `updatedAt` is always written.
- *409 already assigned*: there is no such rule.
- *204*: the controller always answers with `res.json({ issue })`.

readMore.why: How the controller answers an assignment.

notes.title: A new sprint is PLANNED, and the state machine says so first
notes.body:
**Key: 409 "Cannot complete a sprint that is PLANNED (must be ACTIVE)".**

`createSprint` writes only `projectId`, `name` and `goal`; the schema default gives `state` the value `PLANNED`. `completeSprint` finds the sprint and calls `assertTransition('complete', sprint.state)` on line 85. The complete transition starts from ACTIVE, so it throws that message before the guarded `updateMany` runs.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Sprint was already completed*: that comes from line 118, which is not reached.
- *200 with movedCount 0*: the transition check fails first.
- *404 Sprint*: the lookup filters by id and project, not by state.

excerpts.quote: throw conflict(`Cannot ${action} a sprint that is ${currentState} (must be ${t.from})`);

notes.title: null clears the assignee, and a cleared assignee gets no notification
notes.body:
**Key: it clears the assignee and logs assignee.changed, with no notification.**

`if ('assigneeId' in patch) data.assigneeId = patch.assigneeId;` copies `null` into the update (the comment says "null clears"). Inside the transaction, `data.assigneeId !== issue.assigneeId` is true, so an `assignee.changed` entry is recorded. After the commit, the notification needs `data.assigneeId` to be truthy, and `null` is not.

Why the others are wrong:
- *U stays assigned*: only `undefined` means leave alone; `null` is copied.
- *notification to U*: the condition requires a new, truthy assignee.
- *no activity*: the activity check compares the old and new values, which differ.

excerpts.quote: if ('assigneeId' in data && data.assigneeId && data.assigneeId !== issue.assigneeId) {

notes.title: Reading a sprint report is a read permission
notes.body:
**Key: it returns the report, because its default action sprint:read admits VIEWER.**

`loadProject` has the default `action = 'sprint:read'`, and `sprintReport` calls it with no action. In the policy, `sprint:read` lists `ADMIN`, `MEMBER` and `VIEWER`. The writes (`createSprint`, `startSprint`, `completeSprint`, `assignIssueToSprint`) pass `'sprint:manage'` instead.

Why the others are wrong:
- *403*: only the writes ask for `sprint:manage`.
- *404*: the viewer is a member, so the membership check passes.
- *sums hidden from the viewer*: the report has no role-based fields.

readMore.why: The two sprint actions and their roles.

notes.title: Checking that every refusal precedes the first write
notes.body:
The goal is about ORDER: no rejection may happen after `completeSprint` has started writing. The matching Check lists every `throw` before line 114 (lines 83, 85, 89, 95 and 97) and notes that all of them run before `tx.sprint.updateMany`, the first write. It then names the regression that proves the same thing from outside: after a 404 for a cross-project destination, the source sprint is still ACTIVE and the issue is still assigned.

The diff Check is for the exercise about the pre-change gaps, and the predicate-classification Check is for the exercise that sorts predicates into scope, lifecycle and unfinished work.

notes.title: Exact equality pins the future-clock rule
notes.body:
The goal asks you to confirm that the future-clock answer is exact, not approximate. The keyed Check points at `apps/api/test/sprint.test.js:111`, which uses `toBe(captured.getTime() + 1)`: strict equality, not a range. It adds why that matters: a version of line 152 using plain `Date.now()` would be about 60,000 ms off and fail.

The retry-loop Check verifies "three attempts, P2034 only", and the lines 268-274 Check verifies the assignment-versus-completion final state. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

notes.title: Why concurrent starts end in a 409
notes.body:
The goal: explain why the concurrent-starts test expects 409 and not a serialization retry. The keyed Check gives the reason: the two starts update DIFFERENT sprint rows, so the partial unique index is what rejects the second one. That raises P2002, which `startSprint` maps to 409 at lines 68-71. Even if PostgreSQL first reports P2034, `serializable()` retries and the retry hits the same constraint or runs out of attempts; both end in 409.

The other Check, about lines 268, 269 and 274, belongs to the timeline exercise for the never-strands test.

excerpts.quote: so the partial unique index is what rejects the second one.

notes.title: The 30-second waits in the web test
notes.body:
The goal is to find the deliberately long waits in the browser test and say what they protect against. The keyed Check points at `{ timeout: 30000 }` on lines 64 and 67 of `apps/web/test/backlog-stale-assignment.test.jsx`, and explains them: Testing Library's one-second default flaked on a slow host, so the wait was raised while the assertions stayed the same.

The grep Check reconciles the test count (13 + 4 = 17), and the `__realClient` Check explains how the nonmember test proves no mutation. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

notes.title: Match your timeline to the real assertions
notes.body:
The goal: make sure your two-column timeline matches what the never-strands test actually asserts. The keyed Check lists those assertions: completion must return 200 (line 268), the assignment may return 200 or 409 (line 269), and the final `sprintId` must be null (line 274). If your timeline ends with the issue still on the completed sprint, find the guard that prevents it: the COMPLETED check in the service or the serialization conflict.

The other Check explains the different concurrent-starts test, where the unique index, not a retry, produces the 409.

notes.title: Sorting completion predicates by purpose
notes.body:
The goal is to classify every predicate in `completeSprint`. The keyed Check does exactly that: project scope is `projectId: project.id`; lifecycle is `assertTransition`, `target.state !== 'PLANNED'` and `state: 'ACTIVE'`; unfinished work is `columnId: { notIn: doneColumnIds }`. It also asks why the bulk move needs no project filter: `sprintId: sprint.id` names a sprint that was already found inside the project.

The diff Check answers the "what did the old version get wrong" exercise, and the throws-before-line-114 Check answers the ordering exercise. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

notes.title: The race test judges the final state
notes.body:
The goal: confirm the assignment-versus-completion answer is checked on final state, not on the response. The keyed Check points at lines 268-274 of the sprint test: the assignment may return 200 or 409, and afterwards the test reads the issue detail and requires `sprintId` to be null. A test that looked only at the assignment status would miss a stranded issue.

The `toBe(captured.getTime() + 1)` Check is for the future-clock goal, and the `attempt < 3` Check is for the retry-helper goal. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

notes.title: Finding every serializable caller
notes.body:
The goal is to list every service function that runs inside the serializable boundary. The keyed Check is a search: `git grep -n "return serializable("` in the sprint service prints three lines, 46, 81 and 137, one each for `startSprint`, `completeSprint` and `assignIssueToSprint`. The map chapter adds that `listSprints`, `createSprint` and `sprintReport` do not use it.

The `__NO_ROLLBACK__` Check is for the exercise about the test suite opting out of rollback isolation, and the diff Check is for the list-projection wiring gap. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

notes.title: Why the nonmember test reads the database directly
notes.body:
The goal: explain why the nonmember test reads through `__realClient` and not through the API. The keyed Check gives the reason: the outsider's API reads would return 404 just like the write did, so the API cannot show what happened to the row. Querying `__realClient.issue.findUnique` directly is the only way to show that neither `sprintId` nor `updatedAt` changed.

The 30-second timeout Check belongs to the web-test exercise, and the grep Check reconciles the test count with the evidence log. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

excerpts.quote: const stored = await __realClient.issue.findUnique({ where: { id: i1.id } });

notes.title: Reconciling the test count with the evidence
notes.body:
The goal is to reconcile the course's test count with the recorded evidence. The keyed Check counts top-level `it(` blocks: `grep -c` prints 13 for `apps/api/test/sprint.test.js` and 4 for `apps/api/test/issue.test.js`. That is 17, the same number as the `Tests 17 passed` line in the evidence log. Counting yourself is how you check a claim like "17 tests passed" instead of trusting it.

The `__realClient` Check answers the nonmember exercise, and the `{ timeout: 30000 }` Check answers the web-test exercise. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

notes.title: Comparing the two writers that use expectedUpdatedAt
notes.body:
The goal: compare sprint assignment with the OTHER writer that uses `expectedUpdatedAt`, and judge which is stronger. The keyed Check names that writer, `updateIssue` in `issue.service.js`. It reads the issue, compares timestamps in JavaScript, and only then runs an `update` whose `where` is just `{ id }`. Because the compare is not in the write predicate, two requests can both pass it. Assignment, which puts the token in `updateMany`, is stronger.

The line-137 Check labels the three mechanisms, and the lines 96-112 Check computes the future-clock token.

excerpts.quote: The compare is not in the write predicate, so two requests can both pass it.

notes.title: Labelling isolation, guards and the version check
notes.body:
The goal asks you to label which lines of `assignIssueToSprint` are isolation, which are ownership or lifecycle guards, and which are the optimistic version check. The keyed Check does the labelling: isolation is the `serializable(` call (line 137); guards are the project-scoped sprint lookup and the COMPLETED rejection (lines 143-150); the version check is the `updatedAt` term in the predicate (line 156) plus `changed.count === 0` giving 409 (lines 160-162).

The `updateIssue` Check compares writers, and the 60,000 ms Check computes the next token. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.

notes.title: Computing the next token with a fast stored clock
notes.body:
The goal: compute the next token when the stored timestamp is ahead of the clock. The keyed Check points at the test that sets `updatedAt` to `Date.now() + 60_000` and expects exactly `captured.getTime() + 1`, and explains why: `Math.max(Date.now(), previous + 1)` picks the second argument because the wall clock is a minute behind.

The line-137 Check labels the three protection mechanisms, and the `updateIssue` Check compares the two writers that use `expectedUpdatedAt`. The other two choices are real Checks too, but they belong to other exercises in the same chapter, so they verify a different goal.
